clue.text: High time for an English man's excursion .

definitions.text: High time for an English man's excursion

parts.words: High time for an English man's excursion
parts.note: recalls the song line that only mad dogs and Englishmen go out in the midday sun, so the Englishman's outing is at the top of the day

explanation.surface: A suggestion of the right moment for a jaunt by an Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High time' looks like 'about time', but it means the sun at its highest. Noel Coward's song 'Mad Dogs and Englishmen' says they go out in the midday sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is when the sun stands highest, the high point of the clock.

clue.text: Brave granny' has Simon 'up, and about all right

indicators.note: Simon goes about, around, the other piece
in a down clue going up means the letters are read bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: OK is all right

explanation.surface: A courageous grandmother has Simon up and around, feeling fine.
explanation.walkthrough: In Longfellow's 'The Song of Hiawatha', Nokomis is Hiawatha's grandmother; 'Brave' means a Native American warrior. 'about' wraps the name round the short word for all right, and 'up' turns SIMOKON backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiawatha, a young warrior, was brought up by his grandmother in Longfellow's poem.

clue.text: Anyhow' never load with an excessive burden

indicators.note: anyhow means in a careless, disordered way, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Never load anything carelessly with too much weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Carrying too great a load, burdened beyond capacity.

clue.text: One with 'a head, start-led up to an Eastern city

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone given a head start is led up to a city in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: Read in clue order the pieces give IHLED; 'up', in a down clue, turns the whole run backwards, so 'led up to' finishes the city.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital region of India, a city in the East.

clue.text: A long drink

parts.note: a long drink usually means a large glass, but here the vessel is literally long, a tall trumpet-shaped glass of beer

explanation.walkthrough: The yard of ale is a glass about three feet tall, drunk in one go as a pub feat.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall glass holding over a litre of beer, downed as a challenge.

clue.text: Sound of the five o'clock bell provides accompaniment

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five and AM marks a morning hour, so five in the morning
a small bell's sound is a ping

explanation.surface: The chime of a bell at five provides musical backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound of the' tells you to take the noise a bell makes rather than the bell itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To vamp is to improvise a simple repeated backing for a singer or soloist.

clue.text: It masked the point of no return -for Hamlet

definitions.text: It masked the point of no return -for Hamlet

parts.words: It masked the point of no return -for Hamlet
parts.note: in the play's final duel the foil tip is smeared with poison, so the point carries death from which there is no coming back

explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet, Laertes poisons the tip of his foil; 'point of no return' is the sword's deadly point.
explanation.definitionFit: The poison on Laertes' foil tip that kills Hamlet.

clue.text: A one-time TV muleteer ? (He should ring a bell)

definitions.text: A one-time TV muleteer ? (He should ring a bell)

parts.words: A one-time TV muleteer ? (He should ring a bell)
parts.note: a muleteer is a mule driver; the mule here is the puppet Muffin the Mule of early BBC television, and the old street seller of teacakes rang a handbell

explanation.walkthrough: Muffin the Mule was a puppet on 1950s BBC children's TV; the muffin man sold muffins in the street, ringing a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: The street seller of muffins who rang a bell; also read as the handler of Muffin the Mule.

clue.text: Getting one, in the eye is better than this

definitions.text: Getting one, in the eye is better than this

parts.words: Getting one, in the eye is better than this
parts.note: in archery or darts, hitting the bull's-eye scores more than the ring just outside it

explanation.walkthrough: 'one in the eye' sounds like a blow; it is a shot in the bull's-eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The ring of a target next to the bull, scoring less than a bull's-eye.

clue.text: Like the conjecture, one entertained, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken, giving its sound

parts.note: a guest is one who is entertained by a host

explanation.surface: Like a supposition, a visitor might comment.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjecture is something surmised, not known.

clue.text: " Let us all ring fancy's" (Mer of Venice)

definitions.text: " Let us all ring fancy's" (Mer of Venice)

parts.words: " Let us all ring fancy's" (Mer of Venice)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from the song 'Tell me where is fancy bred' in The Merchant of Venice, completed by the word for a funeral bell's toll

explanation.walkthrough: The line in Shakespeare's song is 'Let us all ring Fancy's knell'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the tolling of a bell for a death, which the song rings for Fancy.

clue.text: Call the receiver to go round the estate

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them on the telephone
a fence is a receiver of stolen goods

explanation.surface: Telephone someone to inspect the grounds of a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Receiver' suggests the telephone, matching 'Call', but here it is the criminal who handles stolen property.
explanation.definitionFit: To enclose land with a barrier all round its perimeter, as one might an estate.

clue.text: AS polymorphic as a crowded school?

explanation.surface: Something taking many shapes compared to an overfull school.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits as MULTI FORM: a school with many forms, or classes.
explanation.definitionFit: Having many shapes; and a school with many forms, form being a British word for a school class.

clue.text: Wales's top chairman

parts.note: Cader ..., a Welsh mountain, means the chair of the legendary giant whose name is wanted, so he is the man of the chair on a Welsh summit

explanation.walkthrough: Cader Idris is a mountain in Snowdonia; its name means 'the chair of Idris', a legendary giant.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant of Welsh legend whose seat gives a mountain in Wales its name.

clue.text: They're not taken impartially

parts.note: a partial person takes a position in an argument, so impartial people decline to choose a camp

explanation.definitionFit: Taking one party's part in a dispute is the opposite of being impartial.

clue.text: Vehicle not found on.a ''crash course ?

parts.note: a crash course is an intensive, fast one, so a sluggish carriage has no place on it

explanation.walkthrough: The 'vehicle' is a person who is slow; a crash course is rapid learning.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow person, likened to the old slow coach on the road, is no fit for rapid study.

clue.text: Got together makeshift beds and meals

indicators.note: something makeshift is put together roughly from what is at hand, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Campers rigged up improvised beds and food.
explanation.definitionFit: Gathered or put into one place, a synonym for got together.

clue.text: Catch here in H.P. terms perhaps?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: Something bought on hire purchase may be a trap.
explanation.walkthrough: H.P. is hire purchase, the British instalment plan; its letters with IN and TERMS rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A net is where the catch of small shellfish ends up.

clue.text: Idle timekeepers rattling away to the music ?

definitions.text: Idle timekeepers rattling away to the music ?

parts.words: Idle timekeepers rattling away to the music ?
parts.note: bones are a pair of clappers that keep rhythm in a minstrel band, and idle ones would be sluggish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bones' are percussion clappers played to keep time; the whole word means an idle person, and is also a popular song.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazy person, built from idle and the rhythm clappers called bones.

clue.text: Go the rounds in this shoulder-belt

definitions.text: Go the rounds in this shoulder-belt

parts.words: Go the rounds in this shoulder-belt
parts.note: rounds are cartridges, which sit in a soldier's belt slung over the shoulder, not a beat walked by a watchman

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go the rounds' reads like patrolling; the rounds are ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A belt worn across the chest with loops or pockets for cartridges.

clue.text: Maurois' prickly, if 'silent, colonel

parts.note: Andre Maurois wrote 'Les Silences du Colonel' about a taciturn British officer whose surname is also a thorny shrub

explanation.walkthrough: Andre Maurois' novel 'The Silence of Colonel Bramble' (1918) is about a quiet British officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorny blackberry bush, and the name of Maurois' silent colonel.

clue.text: Turkish soldier as an Indian prince ?

explanation.surface: An Ottoman fighter compared to an Indian ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular soldier in the old Turkish army; and the title of the ruler of Hyderabad.

clue.text: A fair example of ribbon development in the country.

definitions.text: A fair example of ribbon development in the country.

parts.words: A fair example of ribbon development in the country.
parts.note: ribbon development is housing strung along roads, but here the ribbons are wound round a pole at a village fair

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ribbon development' is a planning term for houses built along roads; here ribbons are plaited round a pole by dancers on May Day.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall pole hung with ribbons, danced around at village fairs on May Day.

clue.text: Some gigantic caper

indicators.note: some of the word means only part of its letters are taken, a run from inside it

explanation.definitionFit: A grotesque or playful act, a synonym for a caper.

clue.text: As this clem Clemenceau got his stripes

definitions.text: As this clem Clemenceau got his stripes

parts.words: As this clem Clemenceau got his stripes
parts.note: the French premier Clemenceau was nicknamed after a striped big cat, which is how he earned his stripes

explanation.walkthrough: Georges Clemenceau, French prime minister in the First World War, was nicknamed 'Le Tigre'.
explanation.definitionFit: The striped big cat that gave Clemenceau his nickname.

clue.text: More balmy in a sort of unforgettable way.

indicators.note: put into a sort, a jumble, these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A milder climate, strangely remembered for ever.
explanation.definitionFit: In a way that stays in the memory, an adverb of the unforgettable.

clue.text: The body's. bound to be kept, in case.

definitions.text: The body's. bound to be kept, in case.

parts.words: The body's. bound to be kept, in case.
parts.note: an embalmed corpse wrapped in bandages and kept in a sarcophagus

explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' means wrapped in bandages, and 'case' is the coffin, not 'just in case'.
explanation.definitionFit: An embalmed, bandaged corpse preserved in a case, as in ancient Egypt.

clue.text: More than one spoke to the circle

definitions.text: More than one spoke to the circle

parts.words: More than one spoke to the circle
parts.note: spoke reads as a past tense of speaking to a group, but it is a wheel's rod, from hub to rim

explanation.walkthrough: 'spoke to the circle' sounds like addressing a gathering; it means lines from centre to circumference.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines from the centre of a circle to its edge, like a wheel's spokes.

clue.text: Cherry's. seven-stone husband-to be?:

parts.note: the cherry-stone counting rhyme tinker, tailor, soldier, sailor, rich man, poor man names a husband on each stone, and the seventh is the one wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Seven-stone' suggests a light weight; it means the seventh cherry stone in the fortune-telling rhyme 'Tinker, tailor'.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventh figure counted out in the cherry-stone rhyme for a future husband, after poor man.

clue.text: Kipling's kangaroo. chaser

parts.note: in Kipling's Just So story about Old Man Kangaroo, a yellow wild dog chases him across Australia

explanation.definitionFit: The Australian wild dog, Yellow-Dog in Kipling's tale, who pursued the kangaroo.

clue.text: In time comprehends the endless, way of the world

indicators.note: to comprehend is to include or contain, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: to arrive early is to be in good time

indicators.note: endless means the last letter of the word is dropped

explanation.surface: Eventually one understands the boundless ways of life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comprehends' looks like 'understands', but it means contains; 'endless' cuts the final E off 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Worldly, belonging to this life rather than heaven.

clue.text: One street turns into the port

indicators.note: the letters turn into something new, rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A single road leads into the harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Trieste is a major seaport at the head of the Adriatic in Italy.
